633e2daeb065a0f0: JINJIANG (China), Oct 8 — Beyond its old houses featuring traditional Minnan architecture, Wudianshi Traditional Blocks offers a glimpse of how heritage can be given new life, preserving the past while making it relevant and appealing to younger generations.
Wudianshi Traditional Blocks is a historic cultural district located in Jinjiang, a city in Fujian province in south-east China.

To give young people new reasons to experience the historic neighbourhood, the heritage zone merges intangible cultural performances with modern lifestyle events such as coffee and bakery festivals and e-sports competitions.
According to a Wudianshi Traditional Blocks spokesperson, the approach has been well received, with visitor numbers reaching between 50,000 and 60,000 a day during public holidays.
“As you can see, on one hand, there are the ancient houses to learn about Minnan architecture and culture.

Beyond its old houses featuring traditional Minnan architecture, Wudianshi Traditional Blocks offers a glimpse of how heritage can be given new life, preserving the past while making it relevant and appealing to younger generations. — Bernama pic

“On the other hand, during holidays or regular weekends, we hold many intangible cultural heritage performances or events cobined with coffee festivals, bakery festivals and e-sports tournaments like the National Electronic Sports Tournament that young people might be more interested in, all hosted within the block. These are all ways to attract young people,” she told Asean journalists who visited Jinjiang recently.
Twenty-one journalists from nine countries, including Malaysia, took part in the two-week Asean media programme in China that began on September 15.

The programme covered visits to Nanning, Fujian and Beijing, and also provided the media with an opportunity to gain first-hand insights into China’s approach to preserving its cultural heritage while finding new ways to make historic sites relevant and appealing to younger generations

The spokesperson said nearly one billion yuan has been invested in the development of Wudianshi Traditional Blocks, which was not solely driven by commercial returns but also focused on social benefits and cultural dissemination.

To give young people new reasons to experience the historic neighbourhood, the heritage zone merges intangible cultural performances with modern lifestyle events such as coffee and bakery festivals and e-sports competitions. — Bernama pic

The old houses in the district are not merely preserved as historical structures; they also serve as spaces for the younger generation to learn about Minnan culture and architecture, while contemporary activities help create a more appealing atmosphere for them.
The district is open to the public and entrance is free.
Often described as a ‘living museum of architecture’, Wudianshi comprises more than 130 historic buildings preserving over 500 years of history.

Its red brick walls and swallowtail roof ridges are among the distinctive features of Minnan architecture, while the ancestral halls and villas reflect the history of migration and cultural exchange that shaped the local community.
Some villas also feature South-east Asian and European influences blended with local architectural styles, reflecting the area’s historical links with overseas Chinese communities. — Bernama
792f7ac164bd2d1d: PARIS, Oct 8 — Miniscule but packed with energy, neutrinos charge to Earth from outer space, bringing valuable data on the cosmos, according to research that won this year’s Nobel physics prize.
Here are facts about the subatomic particles observed by prizewinner Francis Halzen of Belgium, as told to AFP by members of his team and other scientists.
What are neutrinos?
With no electrical charge and virtually no mass, neutrinos scarcely interact with other matter and pass unseen through the galaxy and anything they touch — even from one end of Earth to another.
“Every second, without you noticing, 65 billion neutrinos from the Sun flow through your little finger nail,” said the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, in a statement presenting the prize.
“We use them like cosmic messengers,” said Damien Dornic, a scientist at France’s CNRS research institute.
They serve “to examine the core of astrophysical phenomena such as the hearts of stars, or even bigger ones such as the formation of black holes, the collisions of galaxies”, he added.
Antarctic ice observatory
When a neutrino touches the nucleus of an atom, an electric charge is produced, giving off a blue light that can be observed in water or ice.

Halzen and his team installed the IceCube Neutrino Observatory — nearly 5,500 optical sensors hundreds of metres under the Antarctic ice — a dark place free of interference — to observe the light from neutrinos passing through the Earth.
“What IceCube has done is to open a new window to observe the Universe,” said Juan Antonio Aguilar, a professor at Brussels Free University and member of the IceCube collaboration.
“Like the first time a telescope was invented, but this time using these other elementary particles.”
The site took seven years to build and has been collecting data since 2011.
“It’s a completely different way of observing the Universe,” said Paschal Coyle, a researcher at the Marseille Particle Physics Centre.
“You don’t need to point a telescope at a specific place. We look in all directions, all the time.”
The observatory has detected neutrinos with an energy charge about a thousand times that of the Large Hadron Collider, the world’s biggest particle-accelerator.
When the sensors spot an interesting neutrino, a message is sent to other telescopes and sensors around the world, telling them to look in the same direction for further insight.
Where do they come from?
So-called high-energy neutrinos are thought to pass through the universe in straight lines from violent cosmic events such as exploding stars and the areas around black holes.

“We’re starting to see what kinds of sources could emit these high energy neutrinos,” said Erin O’Sullivan, astrophysicist at Uppsala University in Sweden and spokesperson for the IceCube collaboration.
“Our best guess right now is these active galactic nuclei, which are the really supermassive black holes with material around it.”

Unravelling the mystery of the neutrinos’ origin “could even solve other mysteries, such as the origin of so-called ultra-high-energy cosmic rays or even Dark Matter,” said Philipp Eller of Munich Technical University, an IceCube analysis coordinator. — AFP
97db75eb3a96df54: KOTA BHARU, Oct 8 — The story of a Kelantan Peranakan Chinese family preserving the heritage of wayang kulit, the meticulous work of a craftsman bringing characters to life from pieces of cowhide, and the determination of a 10-year-old child to become the next generation of practitioners are proof that the traditional art is still alive.
But beyond these stories lies a crucial question: can wayang kulit remain relevant in a world increasingly driven by technology, changing lifestyles and the evolving tastes of younger generations?

Senior lecturer at Universiti Malaysia Kelantan’s (UMK) Faculty of Creative Technology and Heritage, Mohd Aswawi Isa, believes its survival depends on how far society is prepared to view wayang kulit as a cultural treasure that must be preserved, rather than merely a traditional performance.
“Wayang kulit is not merely entertainment. The performance brings together music, carving, language, storytelling and the culture of the Malay community.
“All these elements make wayang kulit a cultural repository that needs to be preserved and strengthened in line with contemporary needs,” he told Bernama.

According to him, wayang kulit performances once served as a means of bringing communities together, with villagers working collectively to build performance spaces and prepare food throughout the several days of a performance.
However, he said, that spirit of togetherness has gradually eroded as society becomes increasingly detached from traditional culture.
Society’s perception needs to change
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Musicians from the Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association during a ‘wayang kulit’ training session in Kok Lanas. — Bernama pic
Mohd Aswawi said the biggest challenge facing wayang kulit was not merely the lack of young practitioners, but also negative perceptions among certain sections of society towards the traditional art.

Among the negative perceptions, he said, were the beliefs that wayang kulit had no future, was merely a waste of time and could not provide a sustainable livelihood, while some also considered the traditional art haram (forbidden under Islamic law) on religious grounds.

Such perceptions had caused some practitioners to become disheartened and eventually abandon the art, although wayang kulit was not considered haram as long as its performances were conducted in accordance with Syariah principles and did not contain elements contrary to Islamic teachings, he added.

Another challenge, he said, was the growing difficulty in finding dalang (master puppeteers), capable of adapting stories to contemporary issues, in addition to a shortage of musicians and traditional musical instrument makers.
“If this situation continues, it is not impossible that one day wayang kulit will exist only as digital recordings on platforms such as YouTube,” he said.

His view was echoed by Kelantan Department of Culture and Arts (JKKN) director Rohaniza Abdullah, who described the development of wayang kulit in the state as rather bleak despite various conservation efforts being undertaken.

She said the situation was not due to a lack of efforts, but was influenced by several constraints, including limited performance opportunities, a shortage of young practitioners and the small number of wayang kulit groups that remain active.

She said wayang kulit must continue to be brought to the public through regular performances, whether on a large or small scale, to prevent the traditional art from becoming increasingly marginalised.
Practitioners call for more performance opportunities
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Nik Imanuddin Hadeef Nik Izdiharuddin, 10, demonstrates his skills in handling ‘wayang kulit’ puppets when met by Bernama at his home in Kampung Kubang Sipot recently. — Bernama pic

Sharing the same concern, Pija Titir Mas Wayang Kulit Association chairman Mohammad Hafiza Che Ya described difficulties in obtaining performance permits and a shortage of new practitioners as among the main challenges to ensuring the traditional art’s continued survival.

Better known as Pak Chu, he said that although public interest in wayang kulit remained strong, opportunities to stage performances, particularly in villages, had declined considerably compared with the past.

“In terms of audiences and those interested in it, there are still many. The challenge now is obtaining performance permits from the relevant authorities. It is definitely more difficult than before,” he said.
He said wayang kulit performances were now conducted in accordance with Syariah-compliant guidelines, without the elements of ritual worship once associated with the art.
According to him, performances must also be adapted to contemporary developments without sacrificing their original identity.
“If there is a campaign or a particular programme, we incorporate the message into the dialogue and performance. We follow current issues, but present them in the form of wayang kulit,” he said.
He said only three senior dalang were currently still active around Kota Bharu, while another three young practitioners were undergoing training.
“I am worried that without continuous efforts, this art will become increasingly marginalised over the next few years, even if it may not disappear completely,” he said.
Technology as a catalyst
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Chairman of the Pija Titir Mas Wayang Kulit Association Mohammad Hafiza Che Ya or better known as Pak Chu, said that although public interest in ‘wayang kulit’ remained strong, opportunities to stage performances, particularly in villages, had declined considerably compared with the past. — Bernama pic

Meanwhile, in efforts to ensure wayang kulit remains relevant, Mohd Aswawi said UMK had introduced various innovations, including the use of a computer numerical control (CNC) laser cutter to speed up the puppet-making process.
“Previously, it could take three to four months to complete a set of puppets. With the technology, the process can be reduced to about a week without altering the original design,” he said.

UMK has also developed the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to document traditional musical rhythms and translate wayang kulit dialogue from the Kelantanese dialect into standard Malay and other languages.
He said the approach was expected to broaden understanding of the traditional art among audiences from outside the state.
Besides offering courses in traditional theatre and musical instrument making, the university also collaborates with the community to produce more cultural practitioners and entrepreneurs.
Evolving without losing its identity
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Chairman of the Pija Titir Mas Wayang Kulit Association Mohammad Hafiza Che Ya or better known as Pak Chu said performances were now conducted in accordance with Syariah-compliant guidelines, without the elements of ritual worship once associated with the art. — Bernama pic
Mohd Aswawi, however, acknowledged that wayang kulit faced major challenges in attracting younger generations.

Therefore, he said, performances needed to be adapted to contemporary developments through the use of social media, more engaging visuals and content that resonated with people’s everyday lives, without compromising the art’s original identity.
“We can introduce innovations, but the main characters, performance structure and identity of wayang kulit must be preserved.
“If everything is changed to the point that its identity is lost, society will no longer recognise the original form of wayang kulit itself,” he said.
He said social media platforms such as TikTok, YouTube and Instagram had become important channels for extending the reach of wayang kulit performances among younger audiences.
Rohaniza shared the view, saying efforts to attract young people required more creative and interactive approaches in keeping with changing times.

She said the use of social media, more engaging visuals and the incorporation of contemporary issues into performances could bring wayang kulit closer to younger audiences without compromising the authenticity of the traditional art.
She stressed, however, that innovations should not alter the main characters and original structure of the performance to the extent that the identity of wayang kulit was lost.
“Innovations can be introduced in line with changing times, but traditional elements must be retained so that people can still recognise the true identity of wayang kulit,” she said.
JKKN strengthens conservation efforts
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Kelantan Department of Culture and Arts (JKKN) director Rohaniza Abdullah, who described the development of wayang kulit in the state as rather bleak despite various conservation efforts continuing to be carried out. — Bernama pic
Rohaniza said efforts to preserve wayang kulit were being carried out comprehensively through three main pillars — conservation, development and promotion.

She said the approach was implemented through festivals, regular performances, workshops, courses, cultural arts education programmes as well as the documentation of performances and puppet-making techniques, ensuring the heritage remained preserved and could be referred to by future generations.

According to her, the apprenticeship programme based on a mentor-mentee concept, which has been implemented since 2009, had successfully produced dalang, musicians and wayang kulit puppet makers among the younger generation under the guidance of experienced figures and practitioners.

She said JKKN also organised specialised skills workshops on wayang kulit puppet-making while encouraging schools and institutions of higher learning (IPTs) to stage performances and conduct activities related to the traditional art.

The department, she said, also worked with IPTs to conduct research, produce academic publications and provide performance platforms for practitioners, while assisting them in obtaining Cultural Sector Support Grants (GSSK) to strengthen cultural arts development.

In addition, JKKN continues to strengthen cooperation with non-governmental organisations, schools, IPTs and communities through exhibitions, workshops and performances to broaden young people’s exposure to wayang kulit.

Rohaniza said the efforts of the Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association, which involved the entire family, were also worthy of emulation as they demonstrated the important role of the family institution in ensuring that knowledge and skills related to the traditional art could be passed down from one generation to another.
Audiences, tourists prove ‘wayang kulit’ still has a place
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Chairman of the Pija Titir Mas Wayang Kulit Association Mohammad Hafiza Che Ya during a ‘wayang kulit’ training session in Pasir Mas. — Bernama pic

Despite the many challenges faced by practitioners and the continued efforts by institutions to elevate wayang kulit, the traditional art continues to captivate local audiences and foreign tourists who experience its unique performances first-hand.

For civil servant Nik Mohd Azlan Nik Ahmad, 30, watching the shadows of wayang kulit puppets dance behind the screen, accompanied by the strains of the serunai and the beat of drums, never fails to move him.

“Although I am a local who grew up with this art, my admiration for wayang kulit has never faded. The ability of the dalang to bring multiple characters to life single-handedly demonstrates the immense aesthetic value of our heritage.
“This is not merely entertainment from the past, but the identity and soul of the people of Kelantan that must continue to be preserved,” he said.
For Australian tourist Chloe Grace, 45, a wayang kulit performance offers a cultural experience that is difficult to find elsewhere.
“I was truly amazed. It is extraordinary how intricately carved pieces of leather can create such a vivid story through nothing more than the interplay of light and shadow.
“The traditional music seemed to transport me to another world. This is one of the most unique cultural experiences I have ever had,” she said.

The presence of local audiences and foreign tourists demonstrates that wayang kulit can still transcend boundaries of age, culture and nationality, giving it strong potential to be further developed as a cultural tourism product capable of introducing Kelantan’s identity to the international stage.
A heritage that still has hope
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Senior lecturer at Universiti Malaysia Kelantan’s (UMK) Faculty of Creative Technology and Heritage, Mohd Aswawi Isa, believes its survival depends on how far society is prepared to view ‘wayang kulit’ as a cultural treasure that must be preserved, rather than merely a traditional performance. — Bernama pic

The four stories featured in this series demonstrate that the survival of wayang kulit does not depend on a single individual, but is built on the dedication of many parties playing their respective roles.

From the Kang Boon Ann family’s efforts to preserve the heritage across generations, the painstaking craftsmanship involved in creating each puppet from cowhide, dalang Mohammad Hafiza’s dedication to bringing every performance to life, and young apprentice Nik Imanudin Hadeef’s determination to learn the art, to the efforts of UMK and JKKN to strengthen conservation through education, research, innovation and talent development — together, these efforts form a mutually supportive ecosystem.

Although the art faces various challenges, including public perceptions, a shortage of young practitioners, fewer active groups and increasingly limited performance opportunities, all those interviewed by Bernama agreed that efforts to preserve wayang kulit must continue relentlessly to ensure the heritage does not fade with time.

Public support, the enthusiasm of local audiences and the interest shown by foreign tourists are also signs that wayang kulit still has a place in the modern world, provided it continues to be preserved and strengthened in keeping with the times.

As long as there are dalangs willing to share their knowledge, craftsmen dedicated to creating each character, families committed to passing their skills on to the next generation, institutions continuing to strengthen conservation efforts, and communities that never tire of appreciating every performance, Kelantan’s wayang kulit will continue to live on as a cultural heritage that transcends generations rather than becoming merely a relic of history. — Bernama
23163b7197a35430: ISTANBUL, Oct 8 — Ahead of COP31 next month, Turkish NGOs hope the UN climate summit will offer a rare opportunity to be heard in a country where space for public protest has steadily narrowed and arrests can happen “any time”.

Debates, workshops, cultural events and a massive rally are on the agenda for the People’s Climate Summit that will run alongside the main event in the southern Turkish city of Antalya from November 9.

Although hosting COP31 is a major diplomatic win for Turkey, NGOs and civil society groups know the authorities have little appetite for displays of activism or protest that are part and parcel of the annual climate summit.
Last month, police raided the LGBTQ community, detaining 117 people in an “obscenity” probe.
And ahead of July’s Nato summit in Ankara, police rounded up 4,412 people on terror-related charges — including journalists, civil society leaders and over a dozen environmental volunteers.

While it was unlikely there would be a similar pre-summit crackdown before COP31, it fired a warning shot that did not go unnoticed, said Ozlem Katisoz, a senior climate policy coordinator for Climate Action Network (CAN) in Turkey.
“We are not expecting the government to treat COP like Nato, but what happened then showed how quickly and expansively space can be restricted when the government chooses to do so,” she told AFP.
At COP30 in Brazil, tens of thousands marched peacefully, unlike at the previous summits in Egypt, the UAE and Azerbaijan, where NGOs deemed protests outside the UN-run venue unsafe.

For Cigdem Ozbas of the People’s Climate Summit, a grassroots initiative of more than 100 organisations and individuals, COP31 was “fundamentally a gathering of civil society” and not like a Nato summit.
“But in the increasingly authoritarian environment in Turkey, nobody can feel fully secure. Detentions can occur at any time, and often the real reasons behind them are concealed,” she told AFP.
Carnival-like rally

Ozbas said so far, more than 1,000 people had committed to joining the People’s Climate Summit, among them over 300 organisations from 100 countries, who will help “make our demands visible” during the first week.

During the second week, there will be forums, thematic meetings and evening monitoring sessions to “examine proposals that amount to greenwashing, that obscure the real issues, or whose commitments remain unfulfilled,” she said.

US climate organisations were to run “puppet-making workshops” ahead of a major rally on November 14 that will be joined by unions, rights groups and others that will have “a carnival-like atmosphere”.

“The aim is to send a message to decision-makers that we won’t accept decisions made behind closed doors under the influence of lobbyists, authoritarianism, or the pressures of growing fascism,” she said.

Suheyla Dogan, head of the Kazdagi nature protection association that campaigns against mining projects, said they would be demanding “much more concrete and serious policies” from the Turkish government.
“We have the right to assemble and demonstrate and we will do everything we can within the law to exercise those rights,” she told AFP.
Holding Turkey to account
Separately, Climate Network Turkiye — a coalition of 15 top civil society organisations — is trying to get access to negotiators.

Bengisu Ozenc, head of the SEFiA think tank, said they were looking to use their “substantial expertise and knowledge... to influence policy agendas through direct engagement with national policymakers”.
But the summit has not established a formal consultation process, meaning that apart from some individual initiatives “the scope for such influence has remained quite limited,” she said.
CAN’s Katisoz said although the civil society groups had ad hoc relationships with government offices and the COP31 presidency, they were pushing for formalised channels.
“What we need is to be part of the formal policy-making structures at the Climate Change and Adaptation Council in order to have meaningful participation opportunities,” she told AFP.
It was crucial that foreign visitors hold their Turkish hosts to account, she said, and “check what the Turkish presidency is saying with the facts on the ground in Turkey”.
If the Turkish presidency made statements on transitioning away from fossil fuels, delegates should remember there are still new coal plant projects and expansions under way in Turkey.
“The international narrative of the COP presidency should be aligned with the domestic efforts and actions,” she said. — AFP
179ca1ae9c024b81: KUALA LUMPUR: A hospital might seem like the last place you would expect to hear the lively click-clack of mahjong tiles.
Yet just recently, that familiar sound filled the air as Malaysians young and old sat around tables, shuffling tiles, arranging their hands and pondering their next move.
Laughter and friendly chatter abounded as experienced players faced off against newcomers, who were still learning the ins and outs of pongs, chows and kongs.

The session, held in conjunction with World Alzheimer’s Month, was organised by Pantai Hospital and Gray Matter Solutions alongside Jom Mahjong, which bills itself as Malaysia’s first social mahjong club.
Established in April this year, Jom Mahjong aims to bring modern-day Malaysians of all backgrounds together to destress, socialise and make new friends over the centuries-old game.

“I think it’s a great game because it’s very lighthearted and straightforward to learn. Most people can probably pick it up in an hour or so,” Jom Mahjong founder and president Zed Lee, 39, told FMT Lifestyle.
“Many of those who join us say our sessions bring back a lot of memories from when they used to play with their mothers, aunties or other relatives when they were younger.”
Mahjong has been enjoying something of a modern resurgence, with mahjong clubs springing up around the world. It has become particularly popular in the US.

Lee believes several factors have fuelled this renewed interest, including the popularity of the film “Crazy Rich Asians”, which features a memorable mahjong scene, as well as a post-pandemic desire for people to reconnect and socialise in person.
For Lee, the idea for the club struck during a company trip a few years ago, when he found himself playing mahjong with his colleagues.

Despite their differences in age, background and culture, everyone quickly bonded over the game and had a great time. Lee realised then that mahjong could be a simple yet effective way of breaking down social barriers and bringing people together.
As fate would have it, Lee was later gifted an old mahjong table by a relative. Soon he was teaching family members the game, and everyone quickly took to it.
“They taught my other relatives how to play, and sometimes they even play without me!” Lee said with a laugh.
Lee went on to host several mahjong sessions at board game cafés before starting Jom Mahjong. However, fewer than eight people turned up for the first gathering.

Undeterred, he kept the sessions going, and word gradually began to spread. Today, the club hosts between 10 and 12 tables, drawing around 48 players per session. Its largest gathering to date attracted 130 participants.

The club now holds regular gatherings every month, often collaborating with cafés and other venues to bring its social mahjong sessions to different areas. While mahjong may be known as a Chinese game, people of all races and cultures join.
Its members usually play Hong Kong mahjong, one of the most popular variants of the game, although other styles are welcome.

“Beyond the tiles and rules, we want every participant to walk away with a feel for the strategy and a genuine connection to the heart of this tradition and this community we are building together,” Lee said.
While mahjong is sometimes associated with gambling, Lee said “Jom Mahjong” was created specifically so players could exercise their skills at pattern recognition, multitasking and concentration.
For older players in particular, the game is an enjoyable way to keep the mind active and socially engaged, as well as improve cognitive wellbeing.

“It’s a great social game where it’s easy to make friends. I recommend everyone give it a try,” Lee said. “It doesn’t matter if you’re an expert or have never played before, everyone is welcome at the mahjong table.”
Follow Jom Mahjong on Instagram.
a4e6fe13e65a3232: Consumption is no longer just about what we buy. It has found its way into how we measure success.
In our pursuit of more, even the things that once existed simply for pleasure are increasingly expected to produce something in return.
I was sitting near my record player the other day, listening to Janis Joplin sing “Mercedes Benz”, a satire about consumerism and our desire for the good life.
Listening to it now, I wondered if we ever really got the joke, when I was reminded of an old belief of mine.
Books taught me words. They taught me articulation and expression. But songs taught me everything else.
Love, loss, longing, rebellion, disappointment, growing older. Long before I had the language to explain any of it, somebody had already put it into a song.

We still want the car. The house. The title. The salary. The right school for our children. I like nice things too. But somewhere along the way, the things we owned stopped being just things. They became evidence that we were doing well in life.
Then a conversation about reading made me wonder if consumption had moved beyond the things we buy.

A leader I work with had spoken at a conference about the power of reading and the written word. He later shared with a small group of us how the conversation inevitably found its way back to corporate leadership, an idea he gently challenged.
Of course it did.
Even the simple pleasures of reading must now have an outcome to measure.
A book should make us better leaders, sharper thinkers, more employable people. We exercise for performance and network with purpose. Hobbies become side hustles. Even rest needs to be productive.
When did everything, even books, have to earn its keep?
Economics studies what we consume. Psychology helps explain why we want it. Identity is where it gets personal, because what we consume can become part of how we measure ourselves.

We have always compared ourselves with others. We Malaysians are especially good at peering over the fence at relatives with supposedly greener pastures, colleagues and next door neighbours. Now, through social media, we carry millions of other lives around in our phones.
Someone earns more. Someone bought the Mercedes. Someone’s child got straight As. Someone landed a new job or promotion and announced it before breakfast.
The comparisons never end.
Malaysia has its own version of this question. We measure progress through growth, investment, income, infrastructure and development. We should. But what is enough for a country?
Shouldn’t progress also be felt around the dinner table at home?

A decent home. Good schools. Meaningful work. Healthcare we can afford. Time with people we love. Enough money left at the end of the month to breathe, and a retirement fund that makes growing old feel less daunting.

And a book read for no reason other than wanting to know what happens next, such as Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll, where a hookah-smoking Caterpillar asks Alice the rather pivotal question, “Who are YOU?”
Maybe a good life does not need to produce something every minute. Some things should be allowed to exist simply because they make being alive a lot richer.
I looked back at the record spinning beside me.
Janis was still waiting for her Mercedes-Benz.
I think I’ll keep the records. And that wonderfully strange little book about Alice.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
2bee3317e86b71cc: Malaysia merekodkan 28.8 juta pelancong antarabangsa bagi tempoh Januari hingga Ogos 2026, meningkat 1.8% berbanding tempoh sama tahun sebelumnya. Angka ini menunjukkan sektor pelancongan negara terus bergerak dalam arah positif ketika Kempen Tahun Melawat Malaysia 2026-2027 sedang diperkukuh.

Pada pandangan saya sebagai pensyarah dalam bidang pelancongan, pencapaian ini wajar dilihat lebih jauh daripada jumlah ketibaan semata-mata. Pertumbuhan 1.8% tetap positif, tetapi ia juga mengingatkan kita persaingan mendapatkan pelancong semakin sengit. Malaysia perlu memastikan setiap pertambahan ketibaan menghasilkan pengalaman yang lebih baik, tempoh tinggal yang lebih bermakna dan manfaat ekonomi yang lebih luas.

Timbalan Ketua Pengarah (Promosi) Tourism Malaysia, Mohd Akbal Setia, menyatakan prestasi itu mencerminkan daya tarikan berterusan Malaysia sebagai destinasi pelancongan serta kepentingan memperkukuh kerjasama pelancongan antarabangsa. Pandangan ini penting kerana daya tarikan sesebuah destinasi tidak boleh bergantung pada promosi sahaja. Ia perlu disokong oleh produk yang relevan, akses yang mudah dan pengalaman yang memenuhi jangkaan pelancong.

Malaysia mempunyai kelebihan dari segi kepelbagaian. Pelancong boleh memilih pengalaman bandar, makanan, budaya, alam semula jadi, pulau, acara dan aktiviti berasaskan komuniti. Cabarannya ialah bagaimana semua kekuatan ini disusun menjadi pengalaman perjalanan yang mudah difahami dan mudah dibeli oleh pasaran antarabangsa.

Pelancong hari ini membuat perbandingan dengan pantas. Mereka melihat harga, ulasan dalam talian, kandungan media sosial, kemudahan pengangkutan dan pengalaman pengguna lain sebelum membuat keputusan. Oleh itu, destinasi yang menarik tetapi sukar ditempah atau mempunyai maklumat yang tidak jelas boleh kehilangan pelancong kepada pesaing yang menawarkan proses perjalanan lebih mudah.

Dalam hal ini, kejayaan Tahun Melawat Malaysia tidak seharusnya diukur melalui jumlah ketibaan sahaja. Kita juga perlu melihat berapa lama pelancong tinggal, berapa banyak mereka berbelanja, berapa banyak destinasi yang dikunjungi dan sejauh mana perbelanjaan itu sampai kepada perniagaan serta komuniti tempatan.

Berita itu turut menyatakan sektor pelancongan menyumbang lebih 15% kepada keluaran dalam negara kasar. Akbal menjelaskan manfaat pelancongan melimpah ke seluruh rantaian nilai, daripada perhotelan dan perkhidmatan e-panggilan hingga pengusaha kraf tempatan dan restoran milik keluarga. Ini menunjukkan kesan pelancongan tidak berhenti di hotel atau lapangan terbang.

Sebab itu, pengagihan pelancong perlu diberi perhatian. Jika majoriti pelawat hanya tertumpu di beberapa destinasi utama, manfaat ekonomi juga akan tertumpu di lokasi yang sama. Pelancongan yang lebih seimbang memerlukan usaha menghubungkan pelawat dengan bandar sekunder, kawasan luar bandar dan produk komuniti yang benar-benar bersedia menerima pasaran.

Namun, membawa pelancong ke lebih banyak destinasi bukan sekadar isu promosi. Infrastruktur, pengangkutan, kebersihan, keselamatan, papan tanda, akses digital dan kualiti perkhidmatan perlu bergerak bersama. Destinasi yang dipromosikan secara agresif tetapi belum mempunyai kapasiti mencukupi boleh menghasilkan pengalaman negatif dan akhirnya menjejaskan reputasi.

Satu lagi perkara penting ialah kerjasama industri. Penganjuran pameran dan persidangan pelancongan, seni dan budaya antarabangsa atau INTACT 2026 menghimpunkan 154 pempamer dari 35 negara. Menurut Akbal, platform seperti ini penting untuk memperluas promosi bersama dan mewujudkan pengalaman pelancongan baharu yang memberikan manfaat kepada destinasi serta komuniti tempatan.

Saya melihat kerjasama seperti ini sebagai elemen yang perlu diperkukuh. Produk pelancongan jarang dapat dibangunkan oleh satu pihak sahaja. Hotel memerlukan akses pengangkutan, operator memerlukan produk tempatan, destinasi memerlukan pemasaran dan komuniti memerlukan saluran pasaran. Tanpa koordinasi, pelancong mungkin menerima pengalaman yang terpisah-pisah walaupun setiap pemain menawarkan perkhidmatan yang baik secara individu.

Kerjasama antarabangsa pula perlu menghasilkan lebih daripada pendedahan jenama. Pertemuan industri sepatutnya diterjemahkan kepada laluan pasaran baharu, pakej yang boleh dijual, hubungan dengan pengendali pelancongan dan peluang membawa pelawat ke destinasi yang sebelum ini kurang mendapat perhatian.

Pasa masa sama, Malaysia perlu menjaga kualiti pengalaman ketika jumlah pelawat meningkat. Peningkatan ketibaan memberi tekanan kepada pengangkutan, penginapan, tarikan dan tenaga kerja. Jika kapasiti perkhidmatan tidak berkembang seiring permintaan, angka ketibaan yang tinggi boleh disertai aduan, kesesakan dan ketidakpuasan pelanggan.

Atas sebab itu, industri perlu menggunakan data dengan lebih terperinci. Selain angka ketibaan, kita perlu membaca maklumat tentang kepuasan pelancong, aduan, tempoh tinggal, kunjungan semula dan pola perbelanjaan. Data sebegini membantu menentukan sama ada pertumbuhan yang berlaku benar-benar menghasilkan pengalaman yang lebih baik atau sekadar meningkatkan jumlah pengguna dalam sistem yang sama.

Bagi saya, angka 28.8 juta pelancong antarabangsa ialah petunjuk Malaysia mempunyai daya tarikan yang kukuh. Tetapi ukuran yang lebih penting selepas ini ialah kemampuan negara menukar momentum tersebut kepada kunjungan lebih berkualiti. Jika pelancong tinggal lebih lama, meneroka lebih banyak destinasi, berbelanja kepada lebih banyak perniagaan tempatan dan mahu kembali semula, barulah pertumbuhan ketibaan benar-benar menjadi pertumbuhan pelancongan yang bernilai dan mampan.
Penulis ialah pensyarah Fakulti Pengurusan Hotel dan Pelancongan Universiti Teknologi Mara.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
b09373858d7b5301: DETROIT: Leak data posted to the internet has exposed payments made to a hacking group known for extorting large sums of money from law firms, blockchain investigations firm Chainalysis said on Wednesday.

The findings come after an unknown party posted troves of data allegedly associated with Silent Ransom Group, a prolific cyber extortion group. The FBI warned in May that the group was stealing data from law firms through hacks and demanding millions of dollars to prevent it from being posted.

The FBI says the SRG targets specific firm employees with phone calls, emails and sometimes in-person visits to gain access to victims' computers in order to enable access to targeted computer networks.

A website titled "The Luna Moth Files", published earlier this week by an unknown party, posted what it alleged was troves of the group's data, including chat logs, alleged ransom demand totals, documents and other materials associated with the group's work, and dozens of cryptocurrency wallet addresses.

Reuters could not immediately verify the authenticity of the site's claims or data, but Chainalysis said in an X post on Wednesday that "certain leaked SRG addresses sit downstream of millions of dollars in ransomware payments that SRG has extorted from victims".

Chainalysis said certain cryptocurrency addresses contained in the leaks include addresses Chainalysis was already tracking prior to the leak, including one that reflected a US$10 million victim payment SRG collected in mid-2026.
SRG has been alleged to be involved in hacks on prominent law firms including Fox Rothschild and Jones Day, Reuters has previously reported.
2516b2a7c6a75540: NEW YORK: US authorities on Wednesday charged a man who allegedly planned a mass shooting at a shopping mall in Minnesota in support of the Islamic State group.
The FBI arrested Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, after he bought an AK-47 rifle and ammunition from an undercover agent in a sting operation that foiled his apparent plot.
"This individual allegedly obtained a weapon he hoped to use in a mass casualty attack in support of ISIS, but this FBI arrested him and put a stop to his plans," said FBI Director Kash Patel.
Mohamud, from Richfield, Minnesota, allegedly intended to kill 30 to 60 people at the nearby Mall of America - a venue he apparently targeted as he claimed it was Jewish-owned.
He is accused of sharing his intentions with an FBI source in hundreds of messages exchanged since 2024, including a selfie-style video whereby Mohamud pledged his allegiance to IS.
Mohamud allegedly said he wanted to emulate other IS-inspired attacks such as the 2016 Pulse Nightclub Shooting in Florida and the 2025 Bondi Beach shooting in Australia.
He is said to have identified Oct 24 for his planned shooting - saying it would target Asians and other non-Muslims during a planned "Hmong Arts Celebration" at the mall.
"As alleged in the criminal complaint, Mohamud took substantial steps to plot to murder innocent people in the name of ISIS," said Daniel Rosen, US attorney for Minnesota.
Mohamud is charged with one count of knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition in order to commit a federal crime of terrorism. He appeared before a federal judge on Wednesday.
48dd55c2f3733c16: REIM: France's foreign minister Jean-Noel Barrot on Wednesday said his country rejected the "poison" of antisemitism, as he attended commemorations in Israel marking the third anniversary of Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack.

The unprecedented assault led by the Palestinian Islamist movement was the deadliest day in Israel's history. It resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally of official Israeli figures.

"As our societies are confronted with the resurgence of uninhibited antisemitism, we will not allow this poison to spread within the Republic," Barrot said at the site of the Nova music festival in southern Israel, where Hamas militants opened fire around dawn on Oct 7, 2023.
"Everything in France's soul rejects antisemitism and hatred of others," Barrot added.
The minister said the Oct 7 attack "wounded the Israeli people and all Jews to the core and left a trauma that must never be downplayed".
"On that day, Hamas sought to kill the very possibility of coexistence; we will tirelessly continue to work for a just and lasting peace between Israelis and Palestinians," he added.
Barrot also visited Tel Aviv, as well as kibbutz Beeri and Nir Oz, near the Gaza Strip.
In a post on X, he recalled that "51 French nationals lost their lives" on Oct 7.
"We will never forget them," he added in the post, accompanied by a list of victims' names.
During their Oct 7 attack, militants also dragged 251 hostages into Gaza, 44 of them already dead.

In response, Israel's military launched a massive operation in Gaza that has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the territory's health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Antisemitism is a highly senitive issue in France, which has Europe's largest Jewish community.
Jordan Bardella, a leading figure in the far-right which is riding high in polls ahead of next year's elections, recently came under fire over antisemitic comments he allegedly made as a teenager.
The US ambassador to Paris, Charles Kushner, last year accused France of failing to address antisemitism triggered by the Gaza war, leading to a protest by France.
cea9adcc74f9601c: SAN FRANCISCO: Microsoft is pushing a "hybrid intelligence" future with a new Surface Ultra laptop that runs on Nvidia artificial intelligence (AI) chips and will cost more than US$2,500, the company announced Wednesday.

The launch is part of a broader push by tech companies to release hardware that can handle more AI computing on-device and offline, so users don't have to rely solely on remote cloud data centres, where running AI is slower and more expensive.
It also sees Nvidia, whose data centre processors power the AI revolution, make a move into personal computing, a sector dominated for decades by chips from Intel and Qualcomm.

"The trajectory for me is so clear. There will never be a moment where we will go and look and say: 'Oh, this runs locally, this runs in the cloud.' You will expect this hybrid intelligence to be everywhere and pervasive," CEO Satya Nadella said during an event in San Francisco.
He was joined onstage by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who echoed the idea that AI will be integrated into all computing going forward and on all devices.
Agentic AI, in particular, will be central to software development, Huang said, referring to systems programmed to be autonomous and perform tasks without supervision.
With all the changes from AI, "the computer has to be revolutionised," Huang said.
The partnership between the two US-based tech titans helps them compete with Apple, Intel and AMD in the personal computing market.
Apple unveiled two desktop computers in September, the Mac mini and Mac Studio, which it touted as powerful new options capable of processing AI software locally.
Microsoft has been working on building "AI PCs" since at least 2024, when its laptops were powered by Qualcomm chips.
The new Surface Ultra will use Nvidia's state-of-the-art AI chip, RTX Spark, which the semiconductor giant announced earlier this year.
It will cost US$2,599 and begins shipping on Oct 16.
Some AI computing power and data will be processed locally, or on the device, while other applications are still handled remotely via Microsoft's cloud computing services.

57c1fbbcc4f19fb9: If you thought Windows Recall was creepy, buckle up. Microsoft is about to shoehorn even more AI into its desktop operating system, giving Copilot access to every file on your PC. But don't worry, Redmond insists it's totally secure and safe since the agents powering the functionality will run entirely on your PC — some of the time. Microsoft describes the new functionality, announced alongside a new Nvidia N1X powered Surface Laptop, as "hybrid intelligence." Built atop Microsoft's HydraFusion model router, Windows apps and Copilot features will soon be able to use local models when it makes sense and cloud-based models when it doesn't. For example, Windows might use a local model for simple or privacy-sensitive tasks, or decide complex or performance-sensitive requests need OpenAI's GPT-6 or Anthropic's Claude. Local agents will run in Microsoft's Execution Containers (MXCs), agent sandboxes with fine-grained permissions applied at runtime. According to Microsoft EVP of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri, MXCs mean Windows is now "the most secure platform for agents." (That claim will surely age well because models never escape their sandboxes and routers never misbehave.) To support this hybrid intelligence functionality, Microsoft is extending support for Windows ML, its inference framework built on the ONNX runtime, to Llama.cpp – one of the highest-performing inference engines for local AI inference. By adding support for Windows ML, Llama.cpp should be able to take advantage of a broader range of accelerators. Microsoft is rolling out its hybrid intelligence functionality to GitHub Copilot — its AI code assistant — next week and its Copilot app over the next few months. The new Copilot features look and sound suspiciously like OpenClaw in a business suit. Copilot's agentic functionality will not have access to your entire file system, opening the door to advanced search functionality and productivity tasks through integrations with Microsoft Office. In a demo, Microsoft showed how Copilot could be used to find and organize a user's tax documents, then draft an email with those files attached, addressed to an accountant. Microsoft insists it'll only go snooping through your docs if you ask it to. Windows is also getting AI-enhanced search functionality enabling users to surface settings like dark mode. The OS will also get a conversational interface to perform tasks like sending a text message to a friend. Finally, for those interested in coloring outside Microsoft's agentic lines, the company is rolling out a new onboarding experience to make deploying agent harnesses like OpenClaw a bit easier and more secure. Keeping sensitive tasks on device may help to assuage anxieties over privacy, which have dogged Microsoft since the first Copilot+ PCs arrived in 2024 alongside Qualcomm's Snapdragon X Elite SoCs. It should also help to reduce the load on Microsoft's servers by keeping low-priority, low-complexity requests on devices. That said, the impact of running these models locally on battery life, fan noise, and workload quality could prove a turnoff for many users. ®

f92b1ef43b48c0a2: When OpenAI introduced dots last month, it pitched them as "always-on agents" running in their own cloud computer, but that may be overstating the readiness of the technology and of the people trying to use it. Presently, multiple users are reporting task failures and connection issues with their dots. Others have flagged cloud connectivity problems, dots that disappear, and dot refusals that appear to be related to abuse prevention. And the OpenAI Developer Community forum shows several similar concerns. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment about the usage of dots. ABI Research argues that "AI claws" – always-on agents – will shape enterprise AI adoption. The biz sees "a market evolving from isolated assistants toward modular agent ecosystems built for longer-running, enterprise-grade automation." Despite the hiccups that have afflicted dots, some skepticism on social media forums, speculation that OpenAI rushed dots out in response to Meta Muse and Grok Bot, and security issues, dots have some enthusiastic users in addition to detractors who just don't see the point. They also have competition from companies and developers who believe they can deliver a similar service more affordably, with fewer restrictions. A company called Tawkit that makes an SDK called CopilotKit has released OpenDots. "OpenDots is completely open source and gives you the same thing [as OpenAI Dots] as a template you host yourself," the biz said in a post last week. "Bring any agent through AG-UI, use any OpenAI-compatible model, and make every part of it your own." The company previously released OpenMuse and OpenBot. These projects essentially separate the user interface, the AG-UI agent layer, and the backend to provide an alternative personal agent. This doesn't eliminate the token expense of whatever agent is deployed, but it does mean that OpenAI may not be doing the billing. Then there's a potentially lower cost option, called (confusingly) Open Dot, powered by AI models running on OpenRouter. And as it's open source, the code could be altered to run using a local model – a feature that we understand is planned. "Open Dot is an open source version [of OpenAI Dots] that runs on your own Mac with your own OpenAI key, or with open models like Kimi, DeepSeek and Qwen through OpenRouter," the project repo explains. It allows users to connect to various apps like Gmail, Calendar, Slack, Notion, and GitHub via Composio. Prathit Joshi, the project's creator, told The Register, "I enjoy building and shipping tools for developers, especially tools that can support use cases that closed model companies aren't necessarily incentivized to support, like allowing open source models." Joshi is based in Bangalore, India, and works as a growth engineer at Composio. He said he's been using Open Dot to handle personal tasks like setting "to do" lists for the day based on Slack messages and summarizing posts on social media. Open Dot is based on the Electron framework, Joshi said, because he wanted it to be a desktop app. Distinguishing between OpenAI dots, OpenDots, and Open Dot may be confusing, but don't expect things to get any better in the near future. Everyone is busy wrapping increasingly commoditized models in a gatekeeping layer, in the hope of developing a sustainable business. For example, Elon Musk said on Tuesday that Grok Bot would become a model router rather than a front-end for a specific model. "Going forward, SpaceX will use the best back end model for any given task, including Claude Opus 5.5, MidJourney, Suno and other leading APIs," he said. "Whatever is most likely to give you the best outcome." ®

2efb924b3dba3dc9: Researchers at Argonne National Laboratory have plugged an agentic AI platform into an X-ray nanoprobe beamline, creating a system that can get a closer look at areas researchers ask it to focus on. Argonne reported the success of an experimental run of the agentic microscope this week, with the device initially tested on its ability to locate the interface between two regions on an integrated circuit device, and all by just telling the microscope what they wanted it to determine using natural language. “Microelectronics was simply the example used to showcase the technology,” Argonne computational scientist Mathew Cherukara said of the project. “The real achievement is developing a next‑generation, AI‑enhanced microscope that can benefit many scientific fields.” The microscope itself is part of Argonne’s 26-ID hard X-ray nanoprobe beamline, which uses a tightly focused X-ray beam to perform nanoscale imaging and measurements of target samples. Such devices are considered a prime use case for scientific applications of AI because they produce a massive amount of data that can take human researchers considerable time to comb through thanks to their use of a technique known as ptychography. The method collects multiple diffraction patterns as X-rays interact with a sample, with modern X-ray experiments capable of generating millions of images in just a few hours of beam time. Conventional ptychographic reconstruction and analysis can take hours or days, whereas Argonne says its AI system can reconstruct images in real time as the data arrives. Argonne’s X-ray nanoprobe beamline is the sort of scientific facility the Trump administration is looking to boost with AI through its Genesis Mission. Launched by President Trump in November 2025 and led by the Department of Energy, Genesis aims to find ways to use AI in scientific research, including the Synergistic Neutron and Photon Science - Intelligence (SYNAPS-I) project that Argonne is undertaking in partnership with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, which is leading the effort. Brookhaven National Laboratory, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory are also participating in the project. The inclusion of agentic AI in the Argonne X-ray microscope is actually the second phase of the project; the first was simply to see if, as mentioned above, AI could be used to reduce ptychographic image processing time. That was a success, as the lab reported in April, and phase two’s addition of natural language agentic AI appears to have been a win as well. “Combined, these SYNAPS-I advances lay the groundwork for self-driving microscopes, closed-loop experimentation and automated defect-detection tools that promise to accelerate discovery across fields ranging from semiconductor manufacturing to advanced materials and national user facilities,” Cherukara said of the project’s work thus far. In addition to the speed at which the new machine can process data, the conversational AI added in phase two gives researchers the ability to just ask the microscope to examine an area of interest rather than having to figure out how to aim the beam themselves. The AI can not only handle data collection and processing, but also analyze the results itself and flag additional areas of interest, which it can then further investigate on its own. Tao Zhou, a scientist at Argonne, said in a video from the lab that the new, chattier version of the microscope could open up advanced scientific research to researchers who could benefit from X-ray nanoprobe beamline science but don’t know how to operate a complicated instrument like the one at his lab. “This can be a game changer for a lot of users,” Zhou said. “This kind of interactive chat interface allows them to do their scientific research, get excellent data, without having to spend too much time to learn about the beamline components.” “This will help us attract a lot of new users,” Zhou added. Just be sure not to mention toast. ®
4d5e1f5c1fab6083: Artificial intelligence has become part of the zeitgeist. And while it’s a polarizing topic, Linda Rabieh has a unique take on AI: “It’s good for business. Our business, of humanistic thinking.” As senior lecturer in the Concourse program, one of MIT’s first-year learning communities, Rabieh has been introducing students to the “business” since 2010.  “What AI has been useful for is making very vivid to students today the question of what it means to be human,” she adds. “They’re meeting this question with a new urgency. What is intelligence? Is it only mathematical intelligence? Is it only an aggregation of information? Or is human intelligence something different?” AI is just one of countless thorny topics that bubble up in Concourse, which offers first-year MIT students a foundation in the humanities, alongside math and science General Institute Requirement courses taught by Concourse faculty. Studying “great books” and literary luminaries — Plato, Homer, Aristotle, Wordsworth and Coleridge, to name a few — provides a springboard for rich conversations and spirited debates. A “mini-liberal arts college within MIT” Concourse was founded in 1970 to enable humanities, engineering, and science faculty to collaborate on curriculum, cultivating a “concourse” of ideas. Now it’s a place, Rabieh says, “where students who come primarily to MIT for world-class science, math, and engineering can also have a traditional liberal education, exploring fundamental questions of human existence, reading the great books, engaging in intense, vigorous debate about these questions.” “I often describe Concourse as a mini-liberal arts college within MIT,” says Assistant Director Sasha Rickard ’19, an alumna of the program. “A lot of students tell us that Concourse is a big part of the reason they decided on MIT instead of [other schools].” Concourse accepts 50 first-year students each year. Johnnie Jones VI, a senior in mathematics and Concourse teaching assistant (TA) and debate fellow, marvels at the diversity of students the program attracts — “athletes, people who are interested in humanities, people who have no experience in humanities,” he says. “Somehow, 50 people every year self-select into this space, and magic happens.” Connection and “cross-pollination” Part of that magic is the sense of community that Concourse fosters. The program has a dedicated space in Building 16 with a classroom, seminar room, lounge, and kitchen. Students receive advising and participate in community events throughout the year. Since they overlap in their humanities, math, and science classes, as well as outside the classroom, they get to know each other and their instructors well. “There’s a lot of cross-pollination of conversation and ideas,” Rabieh says.  During the weekly Friday advising seminar, students gather over lunch to discuss assigned texts or hold debates. In the fall, topics focus broadly on the human condition, and in the spring, students consider practical political or moral issues such as gene therapy, immigration, and gun control. Several debates are held in conjunction with the MIT Civil Discourse Project, which has collaborated with Concourse since 2023. Many students stay involved in the program after their first year. Some serve as TAs, debate fellows, or associate advisors.  “There’s very much a sense of wanting to be guides and supports and set an example for the incoming students,” Rickard says. Upper-level students also take Concourse electives, hang out in the lounge, and participate in community events. Learning to think things through Taking multiple classes together, sharing meals, and spending time together outside the classroom — these common experiences build a level of trust that allows students to hold deep conversations. The result is a transformative experience. Rickard has noticed that incoming first-years tend to fall into two categories: those who think they already know the answers to political or philosophical questions, and those who have no opinion because they think there’s no definitive answer. Over time, she explains, “some students come to understand that they need to learn from others, and others learn that they really can think for themselves, and they do have something to say.” “Students learn the importance of judgment in non-quantitative areas,” Rabieh says. MIT students excel at quantitative reasoning, she adds, but “you can’t just show which political policy is right and which is wrong … and one reason I think MIT students shy away from those kinds of issues is because they don’t see a way to think through them. Concourse teaches them a way to think about moral and political questions in a rigorous way that isn’t quantitative.” That rings true for Jones. “Overwhelmingly, the greatest skill Concourse has given me, more than just teaching me things, is teaching me how to work through ideas myself — really making possible the ability to, even after a long day of work, sit down with a great book and have a conversation with someone who was alive 300 years ago about things that matter to me,” he says. Stewarding the “ethos of Concourse” into its next chapter As Concourse continues into its next half-century, a new leader has taken the helm. Ford Professor of Political Science Lily Tsai was recently named director after Anne McCants, the Ann F. Friedlaender Professor of History, stepped down. Colleagues laud McCants for 14 years of steady leadership; cultivating a robust, collaborative advising program; advocating for a whole-student approach; and for her passion for teaching. McCants says she relished interacting with Concourse students in a sustained way — often for all four years — and learning not only from them, but also colleagues. “Having a group of committed educators from different disciplines in sustained conversation is a remarkable feature of Concourse. In our normal faculty roles, we are siloed off from those whose fields of study are not ours. I will miss those interactions as much as I do the ones with the students.” Tsai assumes the role as the Institute expands efforts to broaden connections between the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) and other fields. Those efforts include the Compass Initiative, which Tsai co-leads with other faculty from across SHASS; the MIT Human Insight Collaborative; and the creation of shared faculty positions within the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. “The ethos of Concourse is thrilling to me,” Tsai says. “Through reflection and debate about what we value individually and collectively, Concourse students cultivate the skills and habits of mind that prepare them to be not only excellent engineers and scientists, but also responsible citizens and leaders. At a time when the whole world is seeking to ground our use of powerful technologies in thoughtful, principled judgment, Concourse seems all the more vital, and I’m eager to champion the teaching and learning that the program does so well.”

dbae2163d7995bab: Look out, Intel! Microsoft released its first Surface notebook powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark system-on-chip (SoC) during an event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The Surface Laptop Ultra is one of several new Copilot+ PCs powered by the N1X chip that Microsoft says is aimed at "builders," which are available for preorder starting today and expected to begin shipping next week. The machine is arguably the vehicle for a slew of new AI features including hybrid compute functionality that dynamically routes workloads to on-device or cloud models depending on factors like connectivity, privacy, cost, and complexity. The aluminum clad system largely keeps with Microsoft's existing design ethos. It features a high-res, 15-inch mini-LED display capable of reaching a peak brightness of 2,000 nits in Microsoft's signature 3:2 aspect ratio, a standard ten-keyless keyboard layout, haptic trackpad, and a slew of ports including one you won't find on a MacBook Pro. Connectivity includes three USB-C ports, including one equipped with magnets for MagSafe-like connectivity, full-size HDMI, an SD card reader, and a solitary USB-A port because after more than a decade still can't shake the aging connector. But arguably the notebook's most interesting feature is the inclusion of Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X SoC. As we reported earlier this year, these aren't exactly new chips. The N1X is based heavily on Nvidia's now year-old GB10 platform, with a few CPU and GPU cores fused off on lower end models to meet pricing. This tells us that the Surface Laptop Ultra should ship with either an 18- or 20-core CPU designed by MediaTek and Arm and an Nvidia Blackwell-based RTX GPU with between 5,120 and 6,144 cores. In terms of memory, Microsoft says the notebook can be equipped with up to 128 GB of memory, enough to serve large language models up to 284 billion parameters in size, if you can live with just 1.6 bits of precision. As we've previously covered, the GPU is a pretty potent one with a peak theoretical throughput of 1 petaFLOPS at 4-bit precision, not that you're likely ever to see that in many real world workloads. Nvidia's marketing team is leaning on support for 2:4 sparsity to hit that target, so it can theoretically achieve that figure. Unfortunately, almost none of the AI inference workloads anyone cares about these days actually take advantage of the functionality. As a result, the chip's peak performance is actually closer to 500 teraFLOPS, which still gives it an edge over competing chips like AMD's Strix and Gorgon Halo processors. Local AI inference, as we mentioned earlier, is a major selling point for this class of hardware, though Microsoft was also keen to highlight the GPU's capabilities for more traditional creative and gaming workloads, claiming 60 FPS in the latest Gears of War release. We suspect that Nvidia's DLSS AI upscaling tech is probably doing the heavy lifting here. In order to keep the system from overheating, Microsoft says that the Surface Laptop Ultra features a beefed up cooling system with 2.5x more capacity than past Surface notebooks. From the renders we've seen, the extra cooling comes courtesy of a big fat vapor chamber. The Surface is expected to begin shipping next week at a starting price of $2,599 for the poverty-spec gray variant with the lower-end 18-core N1X, 24 GB of unified memory, and 512 GB user serviceable SSD. Jumping up to the 20-core chip, 128 GB of memory, and 1 TB of storage will set you back $5,899, and assuming memory prices haven't gone up even more by then. Alongside the Surface Laptop Ultra, Microsoft also announced a mini PC style development kit based on the N1X priced at $5,999. While by no means cheap, it's still cheaper than the similarly specced DGX Spark, which now retails for $6,950, albeit with 4TB of storage rather than 2TB. The DGX Spark also runs a lightly modified version of Ubuntu, which might be worth the premium for some. If your heart is set on a high-memory config and you don't want to wait for the Surface Laptop Ultra to come back in stock, Lenovo, Asus, Dell, MSI, and HP all are launching similarly specced systems over the next week or so. And if Nvidia isn't your style, it's worth mentioning that AMD has its own AI-tuned chips, which now support up to 192 GB of unified memory, and we strongly suspect will support many of the same hybrid AI features rolling out to Windows 11 over the next few months. ®

49ddff06e551479a: Imagine going to a Google website at its correct URL, only to be redirected to a crim's illegitimate copy. Attackers hijacked top-level domains, allowing them to alter DNS records and mint fraudulent HTTPS certificates for several Google domains, and those belonging to other organizations. Google said it became aware of the series of attacks last week in the .gh (Ghana), .sl (Sierra Leone), and .as (American Samoa) country-code top-level namespaces (ccTLDs). “During these hijacks, attackers modified authoritative DNS records and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering several Google domains, as well as domains belonging to other organizations,” Google security warned on Tuesday. Google did not say which specific domains or organizations were affected. The attacks did not compromise Google’s systems, and Chrome quickly blocked suspected counterfeit certificates across the affected ccTLDs - meaning Chrome browser users are already protected - according to the Chocolate Factory. “Due to the nature of the attacks, we have no reason to believe the Certification Authorities (CAs) that issued the impacted certificates did anything wrong,” the alert said. These types of attacks allow criminals to impersonate legitimate organizations and websites without triggering any browser security alerts. The attacker controls the traffic routing (via DNS) and the private key associated with the unauthorized certificate, which means they can potentially intercept or modify data sent by users to the impersonated site - and abuse the trusted organization's brand to distribute malware or conduct phishing attacks. “While Chrome took steps during these incidents to identify and block suspected unauthorized certificates across the affected ccTLDs, browser-side intervention should not be relied on to protect your users,” Google warned domain owners. “Due to the complexity of DNS hijacks, we cannot guarantee that our analysis identified every affected domain, nor do Chrome interventions reliably protect non-Chrome users.” To ensure that their domains and users are protected, Google recommends ongoing monitoring of Certificate Transparency (CT) logs across all of an organization’s domains, including parked or regional ccTLD properties. This provides near real-time alerts whenever someone obtains a certificate for one of your domains. And if you operate a domain in .gh, .sl, or .as, definitely review recent CT log entries for unexpected certificates. Organizations can also publish restrictive Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS records, which allow domain owners to specify which CAs are permitted to issue certificates for their domains. While this won’t stop certificates from being issued during a DNS hijacking attack, it helps safeguard domains after DNS control is restored. Google recommends CAA policies that restrict issuance to specific authorized accounts and validation methods and prevent attackers from using cached validation state to mint new certificates after a hijacking ends.®
8588cf61af9ff366: A phishing campaign targeting advertising managers by impersonating Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Manus to steal credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes has added a fake Muse Ads product to its lure lineup – just eight days after Meta launched its personal AI agent. Meta announced Muse on September 8, and by September 17, a very convincing website – museads.ai – for a product called Muse Ads that promised to help advertisers reach buyers and run sponsored placements popped up online. “The operators already had the platform, so adapting it to a new brand can take minutes,” Oleg Zaytsev, lead security researcher at Island, told The Register. “The striking part is how quickly they turned a timely announcement into a credible reason for someone to act. The same platform could then be repackaged around other familiar tasks, from connecting a business tool to claiming a refund or applying for a job.” The security startup spotted the Muse Ads webpage, and upon digging into the scam uncovered that just the page was new. “Its code, from the sign-in forms to the fake browser window, came from a wider operation that had already run fake ad products for Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Manus,” Zaytsev and fellow Island researcher Ofek Ronen wrote in a blog post published Tuesday. All of these products served as lures for browser-in-the-browner (BitB) attacks designed to trick agency staff, media buyers, and manager-account administrators into handing over their advertising account credentials – along with stored payment methods and client accounts – to digital thieves. “For victims, the potential cost is loss of access to an advertising account, unauthorized ad spend, and exposure of linked client accounts,” Zaytsev told The Register. How the scam works BitB is a clever phishing technique originally detailed by a researcher called mr.d0x in 2022. It involves building a fake login window directly inside a legitimate one. The fake window looks like the real thing, featuring an address bar, title, and URL, but it's just an overlay to steal users’ credentials. According to Zaytsev, this one has likely proved very lucrative for its criminal operators, with hundreds of victim submissions to the platform, and activity still ongoing. “From one frontend alone, we observed submissions involving roughly 200 distinct email addresses over about a month,” he told us. “The operators used the same platform across many similar sites, so we estimate the campaign-wide volume is substantially higher.” Each phony ad product has its own page, with ChatGPT promising users a Monday Google Ads brief, Gemini offering manager account and linked-client support, Claude an advertising portal, Perplexity pitching campaign planning and spend audits, and Manus providing a private Meta integration. Each fake product page also has a “connect” button. When the victim clicks “connect,” it opens the browser-in-browser overlay, with a fake address bar showing accounts.google.com, or an Okta tenant to gain the victim’s trust. The real browser, however, stays on the phishing domain and steals credentials when the victim types them in. A human operator running the campaign sees each submission and chooses what the victim sees and is prompted to do. This includes asking for another password, requesting an SMS or Okta authenticator code to bypass MFA, showing a Google approval code or Okta push request, or displaying a QR code. The platform supports Google, Meta, TikTok, and Okta workflows, and the browser overlay adapts to whatever the victim runs: Window, macOS, iOS, ot Android, and even mimics Safari’s URL pill, Chrome’s custom tabs, and a dark mode. And while the researchers told us they haven’t identified the people operating the kit or found a name under which it’s sold, the operators did expose older source code through misconfigured public GitHub repositories that connected this to a campaign to a larger operation. In addition to the AI ad pages, this operation also used fake refund claims and job recruitment sites as lures with separate builds for Adidas, Google Careers, Robert Half, Tesla, and Louis Vuitton. All of these pages run on one Next.js and Socket.IO stack. Many of the pages also used Vercel frontends with Railway or Render services behind them for state and commands. “A new brand or polished page doesn’t necessarily mean a new attack. Operators can change the lure quickly, but the workflow still has to move someone onto a site they control, collect credentials, and steer them through authentication,” Zaytsev said. “Security teams should maintain a continuous baseline of trusted domains, check the real browser address, and connect similar behavior across different sites,” he added. “Attackers can generate a convincing website quickly; building the domain history and reputation of a legitimate service is much harder. AI can help defenders keep pace with AI-generated websites, especially as they become more convincing and appear more quickly.”. ®

8373a76c0750b53d: Life is remarkably selective. Life relies on many molecules with what is termed "handedness"—they're chemically identical but are mirror images of each other. Most chemical reactions will make a 50-50 mix of the left- and right-handed forms of a chemical, but life uses only one of them. In fact, because of the differences between left- and right-handed chemicals, most of the key enzymes used by organisms will fail to work if they're presented with chemicals that have the wrong handedness.

That poses a bit of a challenge for origin-of-life research, as we're forced to explain how a world that may have started with an even mix of left- and right-handed chemicals produced organisms that only used one of them.

Today's Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to two individuals, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai, who discovered chemical reactions could be biased, producing large excesses of one of the two forms of a chemical.
